parole.testo: Borrowed from Latin alphabētum, from Byzantine Greek ἀλφάβητον (alphábēton), from Ancient Greek ἀλφάβητος (alphábētos), from ἄλφα (álpha, “alpha”) + βῆτᾰ (bêtă, “beta”) + -ος (-os).

Variant of dialectal berniz, from Medieval Latin vernicem (“sandarac, resin”) from veronicem, from Byzantine Greek [Term?], from Ancient Greek βερενίκιον (bereníkion, “soda”), βερονίκιον (beroníkion), from Βερενίκη (Bereníkē). Cognate with English varnish.

Borrowed from Medieval Latin sclavus (“slave”), from Late Latin Sclavus (“a Slav”), from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos) (or borrowed from the Greek directly), see that entry for more. Doublet of eslavo.
Borrowed from Medieval Latin Slavus, from Sclavus, from Byzantine Greek Σκλάβος (Sklábos), which see for more. Doublet of esclavo.
Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin stigmatizō, from Byzantine Greek στιγματίζω (stigmatízō), from Ancient Greek στίγμα (stígma, “tattoo, mark”).

parole.significato: to clarify a concept, to be more specific
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin matizare, from Byzantine Greek λαμματίζειν (lammatízein), from λάμμα (lámma) (for λῶμα (lôma, “band, trimming, edge”)).
From Latin Melchita, from Byzantine Greek Μελχίτης (Melkhítēs), from Classical Syriac ܡܠܟܝܐ (malkāyāʾ, “royal; royalist”) + Byzantine Greek -ῑ́της (-ī́tēs). See these for more.

parole.significato: metaphysics (branch of philosophy that studies first principles)
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin metaphysica, methephisica, from Byzantine Greek μεταφυσικά (metaphusiká). See English metaphysics for further etymology.

Borrowed from Late Latin patriarcha, from Byzantine Greek πατριάρχης (patriárkhēs, “the founder of the tribe/family”), from Ancient Greek πατριά (patriá, “generation, ancestry, descent, tribe, family”) + -άρχης (-árkhēs, “-arch”).

parole.significato: said of a type of pilgrim heading to Rome, or having a certain type of cloak or stick
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin Rōmaeus, from Byzantine Greek ῥωμαῖος (rhōmaîos, literally “Roman”), a sobriquet given to Roman Catholic pilgrims to the Holy Land.
From Latin opalus, from Byzantine Greek ὀπάλλιος (opállios), from Sanskrit उपल (upala, “gem, stone”).
